//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Lisbon_Oriente_Station_%2842264380264%29.jpg/440px-Lisbon_Oriente_Station_%2842264380264%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5472" data-file-height="3648" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Gare_do_Oriente" title="Gare do Oriente">Gare do Oriente</a> train station in <a href="/wiki/Lisbon" title="Lisbon">Lisbon</a>.</div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:222px;max-width:222px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Metro_do_Porto_-_MP_100_(6289259423).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Metro_do_Porto_-_MP_100_%286289259423%29.jpg/220px-Metro_do_Porto_-_MP_100_%286289259423%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Metro_do_Porto_-_MP_100_%286289259423%29.jpg/330px-Metro_do_Porto_-_MP_100_%286289259423%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Metro_do_Porto_-_MP_100_%286289259423%29.jpg/440px-Metro_do_Porto_-_MP_100_%286289259423%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4288" data-file-height="2848" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Metro_do_Porto" class="mw-redirect" title="Metro do Porto">Metro do Porto</a> <a href="/wiki/Bombardier_Flexity_Swift" class="mw-redirect" title="Bombardier Flexity Swift">Bombardier Flexity Swift</a> train in <a href="/wiki/Maia,_Portugal" title="Maia, Portugal">Maia</a>.</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>By the early-1970s, Portugal's <a href="/wiki/Economic_history_of_Portugal" title="Economic history of Portugal">fast economic growth</a> with increasing <a href="/wiki/Mass_consumption" class="mw-redirect" title="Mass consumption">consumption</a> and purchase of new automobiles set the priority for improvements in transportation. Again in the 1990s, after joining the <a href="/wiki/European_Economic_Community" title="European Economic Community">European Economic Community</a>, the country built many new motorways. Today, the country has a 68,732&#160;km (42,708&#160;mi) road network, of which almost 3,000&#160;km (1,864&#160;mi) are part of system of 44 motorways. Opened in 1944, the first motorway (which linked Lisbon to the National Stadium) was an innovative project that made Portugal one of the first countries in the world to establish a motorway (this roadway eventually became the Lisbon-Cascais highway, or A5).
</p><p>Although a few other tracts were created (around 1960 and 1970), it was only after the beginning of the 1980s that large-scale motorway construction was implemented. In 1972, <a href="/wiki/BRISA_Auto-estradas_de_Portugal_S.A." class="mw-redirect" title="BRISA Auto-estradas de Portugal S.A.">Brisa</a>, the highway concessionaire, was founded to handle the management of many of the region's motorways. On many highways, a toll needs to be paid (see <a href="/wiki/Via_Verde" title="Via Verde">Via Verde</a>). <a href="/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama_bridge" class="mw-redirect" title="Vasco da Gama bridge">Vasco da Gama bridge</a> is the longest bridge in the <a href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">EU</a> (the second longest in Europe) at 12.345&#160;km.<sup id="cite_ref-259" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-259">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-260" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-260">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Continental_Portugal" title="Continental Portugal">Continental Portugal</a>'s 89,015&#160;km<sup>2</sup> (34,369&#160;sq&#160;mi) territory is serviced by four international airports located near the principal cities of <a href="/wiki/Lisbon" title="Lisbon">Lisbon</a>, <a href="/wiki/Porto" title="Porto">Porto</a>, <a href="/wiki/Faro,_Portugal" title="Faro, Portugal">Faro</a> and <a href="/wiki/Beja_(Portugal)" class="mw-redirect" title="Beja (Portugal)">Beja</a>. Lisbon's geographical position makes it a stopover for many foreign airlines at several airports within the country. The primary <a href="/wiki/Flag-carrier" class="mw-redirect" title="Flag-carrier">flag-carrier</a> is <a href="/wiki/TAP_Air_Portugal" title="TAP Air Portugal">TAP Air Portugal</a>, although many other domestic airlines provide services within and without the country. The government decided to build a new airport outside Lisbon, to replace <a href="/wiki/Lisbon_Portela_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Lisbon Portela Airport">Lisbon Portela Airport</a>, though this plan has been suspended due to austerity measures. Currently, the most important airports are in <a href="/wiki/Portela_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Portela Airport">Lisbon</a>, <a href="/wiki/Francisco_S%C3%A1_Carneiro_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Francisco Sá Carneiro Airport">Porto</a>, <a href="/wiki/Faro_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Faro Airport">Faro</a>, <a href="/wiki/Madeira_Airport" title="Madeira Airport">Funchal</a> (Madeira), and <a href="/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_Paulo_II_Airport" title="João Paulo II Airport">Ponta Delgada</a> (Azores), managed by the national airport authority group <a href="/wiki/ANA_%E2%80%93_Aeroportos_de_Portugal" class="mw-redirect" title="ANA – Aeroportos de Portugal">ANA&#160;– Aeroportos de Portugal</a>. One other important airport is the Aeroporto Internacional das Lajes on the island of Terceira in the Azores. This airport serves as one of two international airports serving countries outside the European Union for all nine islands of the Azores. It also serves as a military air base for the United States Air Force. The base remains in use to the present day.
</p><p>A national railway system that extends throughout the country and into Spain, is supported and administered by <a href="/wiki/Comboios_de_Portugal" title="Comboios de Portugal">Comboios de Portugal</a> (CP). <a href="/wiki/Rail_transport" title="Rail transport">Rail transport</a> of passengers and goods is derived using the 2,791&#160;km (1,734&#160;mi) of railway lines currently in service, of which 1,430&#160;km (889&#160;mi) are electrified and about 900&#160;km (559&#160;mi) allow train speeds greater than 120&#160;km/h (75&#160;mph). The railway network is managed by <a href="/wiki/Infraestruturas_de_Portugal" title="Infraestruturas de Portugal">Infraestruturas de Portugal</a> while the transport of passengers and goods are the responsibility of CP, both public companies. In 2006, the CP carried 133,000,000 passengers and 9,750,000 <a href="/wiki/Tonne" title="Tonne">tonnes</a> (9,600,000 <a href="/wiki/Long_ton" title="Long ton">long tons</a>; 10,700,000 <a href="/wiki/Short_ton" title="Short ton">short tons</a>) of goods.
</p><p>The major seaports are located in <a href="/wiki/Sines,_Portugal" class="mw-redirect" title="Sines, Portugal">Sines</a>, <a href="/wiki/Lisbon" title="Lisbon">Lisbon</a>, <a href="/wiki/Leix%C3%B5es" title="Leixões">Leixões</a>, <a href="/wiki/Set%C3%BAbal" title="Setúbal">Setúbal</a>, <a href="/wiki/Aveiro,_Portugal" title="Aveiro, Portugal">Aveiro</a>, <a href="/wiki/Figueira_da_Foz" title="Figueira da Foz">Figueira da Foz</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Faro,_Portugal" title="Faro, Portugal">Faro</a>.
</p><p>The two largest metropolitan areas have subway systems: <a href="/wiki/Lisbon_Metro" title="Lisbon Metro">Lisbon Metro</a> and <i>Metro Sul do Tejo</i> in the <a href="/wiki/Lisbon_metropolitan_area" title="Lisbon metropolitan area">Lisbon metropolitan area</a> and <a href="/wiki/Porto_Metro" title="Porto Metro">Porto Metro</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Porto_Metropolitan_Area" class="mw-redirect" title="Porto Metropolitan Area">Porto Metropolitan Area</a>, each with more than 35&#160;km (22&#160;mi) of lines. In Portugal, <a href="/wiki/Trams_in_Lisbon" title="Trams in Lisbon">Lisbon tram services</a> have been supplied by the <i>Companhia de Carris de Ferro de Lisboa</i> (<a href="/wiki/Carris" title="Carris">Carris</a>), for over a century. In <a href="/wiki/Porto" title="Porto">Porto</a>, <a href="/wiki/Trams_in_Porto" title="Trams in Porto">a tram network</a>, of which only a tourist line on the shores of the <a href="/wiki/Douro" title="Douro">Douro</a> remains, began construction on 12 September 1895 (a first for the <a href="/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula" title="Iberian Peninsula">Iberian Peninsula</a>). All major cities and towns have their own local urban transport network, as well as taxi services.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Energy">Energy</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=36" title="Edit section: Energy">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Energy_in_Portugal" title="Energy in Portugal">Energy in Portugal</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:224px;max-width:224px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:222px;max-width:222px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Serra_da_Freita_-_Portugal_(51991153152).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Serra_da_Freita_-_Portugal_%2851991153152%29.jpg/220px-Serra_da_Freita_-_Portugal_%2851991153152%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Serra_da_Freita_-_Portugal_%2851991153152%29.jpg/330px-Serra_da_Freita_-_Portugal_%2851991153152%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Serra_da_Freita_-_Portugal_%2851991153152%29.jpg/440px-Serra_da_Freita_-_Portugal_%2851991153152%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1365" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Wind_farm" title="Wind farm">Wind farm</a> in Serra da Freita, <a href="/wiki/Arouca,_Portugal" title="Arouca, Portugal">Arouca</a>.</div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:222px;max-width:222px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Alqueva_dam.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Alqueva_dam.JPG/220px-Alqueva_dam.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Alqueva_dam.JPG/330px-Alqueva_dam.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Alqueva_dam.JPG/440px-Alqueva_dam.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1200" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Alqueva_Dam" title="Alqueva Dam">Alqueva Dam</a>, the largest dam and artificial lake in Western Europe.</div></div></div></div></div>
<p>Portugal has considerable resources of wind and river power, the two most cost-effective renewable energy sources. Since the turn of the 21st century, there has been a trend towards the development of a renewable resource industry and reduction of both consumption and use of fossil fuels. In 2006, the world's largest <a href="/wiki/Solar_energy" title="Solar energy">solar power</a> plant at that date, the <a href="/wiki/Moura_Photovoltaic_Power_Station" title="Moura Photovoltaic Power Station">Moura Photovoltaic Power Station</a>, began operating near <a href="/wiki/Moura,_Portugal" title="Moura, Portugal">Moura</a>, in the south, while the world's first commercial <a href="/wiki/Wave_power" title="Wave power">wave power</a> farm, the <a href="/wiki/Agu%C3%A7adoura_Wave_Farm" title="Aguçadoura Wave Farm">Aguçadoura Wave Farm</a>, opened in the <a href="/wiki/Norte_Region,_Portugal" class="mw-redirect" title="Norte Region, Portugal">Norte region</a> (2008). By the end of 2006, 66% of the country's electrical production was from coal and fuel power plants, while 29% were derived from <a href="/wiki/Hydroelectric" class="mw-redirect" title="Hydroelectric">hydroelectric</a> dams, and 6% by <a href="/wiki/Wind_energy" class="mw-redirect" title="Wind energy">wind energy</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-261" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-261">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2008, renewable energy resources were producing 43% of the nation's consumption of electricity, even as hydroelectric production decreased with severe droughts.<sup id="cite_ref-262" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-262">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup> As of June 2010, electricity exports had outnumbered imports. In the period between January and May 2010, 70% of the national production of energy came from renewable sources.<sup id="cite_ref-263" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-263">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Portugal's national energy transmission company, <a href="/wiki/Redes_Energ%C3%A9ticas_Nacionais" title="Redes Energéticas Nacionais">Redes Energéticas Nacionais</a> (REN), uses sophisticated modelling to predict weather, especially wind patterns, and computer programs to calculate energy from the various renewable-energy plants.
Before the solar/wind revolution, Portugal had generated electricity from hydropower plants on its rivers for decades. New programmes combine wind and water: wind-driven turbines pump water uphill at night, the most blustery period; then the water flows downhill by day, generating electricity, when consumer demand is highest. Portugal's distribution system is also now a two-way street. Instead of just delivering electricity, it draws electricity from even the smallest generators, like rooftop solar panels. The government aggressively encouraged such contributions by setting a premium price for those who buy rooftop-generated solar electricity.
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Demographics">Demographics</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=37" title="Edit section: Demographics">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Demographics_of_Portugal" title="Demographics of Portugal">Demographics of Portugal</a> and <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_people" title="Portuguese people">Portuguese people</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tleft"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:204px;max-width:204px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Viana_do_Castelo,_Portugal_(4922364383).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Viana_do_Castelo%2C_Portugal_%284922364383%29.jpg/200px-Viana_do_Castelo%2C_Portugal_%284922364383%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Viana_do_Castelo%2C_Portugal_%284922364383%29.jpg/300px-Viana_do_Castelo%2C_Portugal_%284922364383%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Viana_do_Castelo%2C_Portugal_%284922364383%29.jpg/400px-Viana_do_Castelo%2C_Portugal_%284922364383%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2369" data-file-height="1777" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption">People in traditional attire from <a href="/wiki/Minho_(province)" class="mw-redirect" title="Minho (province)">Minho</a></div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Fado1_-_Fadistas_a_los_Jeronimos.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Fado1_-_Fadistas_a_los_Jeronimos.JPG/200px-Fado1_-_Fadistas_a_los_Jeronimos.JPG" decoding="async" width="200" height="150" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Fado1_-_Fadistas_a_los_Jeronimos.JPG/300px-Fado1_-_Fadistas_a_los_Jeronimos.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Fado1_-_Fadistas_a_los_Jeronimos.JPG/400px-Fado1_-_Fadistas_a_los_Jeronimos.JPG 2x" data-file-width="2272" data-file-height="1704" /></a></span></div><div class="thumbcaption"><a href="/wiki/Fado" title="Fado">Fadistas</a> playing at <a href="/wiki/Jer%C3%B3nimos_Monastery" title="Jerónimos Monastery">Jerónimos Monastery</a></div></div></div></div></div>
<p>The Statistics Portugal (<a href="/wiki/Portuguese_language" title="Portuguese language">Portuguese</a>: <i lang="pt">INE – <a href="/wiki/Instituto_Nacional_de_Estat%C3%ADstica_(Portugal)" title="Instituto Nacional de Estatística (Portugal)">Instituto Nacional de Estatística</a></i>) estimates that, by 31 December 2022, the population was 10,467,366 (of which 52.2% was female and 47.8% was male).<sup id="cite_ref-auto2_11-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-auto2-11">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-264" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-264">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup> The median life expectancy in 2022 was 82.47 years.<sup id="cite_ref-265" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-265">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup>
This population has been relatively homogeneous for most of its history: a single religion (Roman Catholicism) and a single language have contributed to this ethnic and national unity.<sup id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-266">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The most important demographic influence in the modern Portuguese seems to be the oldest one; current interpretation of <a href="/wiki/Y-chromosome" class="mw-redirect" title="Y-chromosome">Y-chromosome</a> and <a href="/wiki/MtDNA" class="mw-redirect" title="MtDNA">mtDNA</a> data suggests that the Portuguese have their origin in <a href="/wiki/Paleolithic" title="Paleolithic">Paleolithic</a> peoples that began arriving to the European continent around 45,000 years ago. All subsequent migrations did leave an impact, genetically and culturally, but the main population source of the Portuguese is still Paleolithic. Genetic studies show Portuguese populations not to be significantly different from other European populations.<sup id="cite_ref-267" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-267">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup> Portuguese people have a preponderancy of genetics (Iron Age Period)<sup id="cite_ref-:0_268-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-268">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup> which belong to R1b haplogroup family along with <a href="/wiki/Brittonic_languages" title="Brittonic languages">Brythonic</a>, <a href="/wiki/Alpine_states" title="Alpine states">Alpine</a> and <a href="/wiki/Goidelic_languages" title="Goidelic languages">Goidelic</a> genetical markers. Also expectable but not so common are South European (Sardinian, Italian and Balkans), broadly North-western (West Germanic) and to a lesser extent British/Irish (Brythonic/Gaelic) and French (Alpine). With a low confidence range there are <a href="/wiki/Scandinavian_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Scandinavian people">Scandinavian</a> and East European genetical markers.<sup id="cite_ref-:0_268-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-268">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup> Other sources would point out a small presence of <a href="/wiki/Berbers" title="Berbers">Berber</a> and Jewish that would be also part of a low confidence region.<sup id="cite_ref-269" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-269">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Native Portuguese are an <a href="/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula" title="Iberian Peninsula">Iberian</a> ethnic group and they form 95% of the whole population,<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> whose ancestry is very similar to Spaniards and have strong ties with fellow <a href="/wiki/Atlantic_Europe" title="Atlantic Europe">Atlantic Arc countries</a> like Ireland, British Isles, France and Belgium due to maritime trade dated as far back as the Bronze Age. These maritime contacts and the prevalence of R1b haplogroup as the main genetical marker of these countries suggest a common ancestry and cultural proximity. Other maritime contacts with the Mediterranean especially with Greeks, Phoenicians, Romans and Moors added some phenotypes in southern Portugal and particularly southern Spain (the <a href="/wiki/Tartessos" title="Tartessos">Tartessos</a> culture), making Portugal and north-western Spain a bridge between north-western Europe and the Mediterranean but maintaining the Atlantic character.
</p><p>Despite good economic development in the past three decades, the Portuguese have been the shortest in Europe since 1890. This emerging height gap took place in the 1840s and has increased since. One of the driving factors was the modest real wage development, given the late industrialization and economic growth in Portugal compared to the European core. Another determinant was the delayed <a href="/wiki/Human_capital" title="Human capital">human capital</a> formation.<sup id="cite_ref-270" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-270">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The total fertility rate (TFR) as of 2015<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup> was estimated at 1.52 children born/woman, one of the lowest in the world, which is below the replacement rate of 2.1,<sup id="cite_ref-271" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-271">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup> it remains considerably below the high of 5.02 children born per woman in 1911.<sup id="cite_ref-272" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-272">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup> In 2016, 52.8% of births were to unmarried women.<sup id="cite_ref-273" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-273">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup>
Like most Western countries, Portugal has to deal with low fertility levels: the country has experienced a <a href="/wiki/Sub-replacement_fertility_rate" class="mw-redirect" title="Sub-replacement fertility rate">sub-replacement fertility rate</a> since the 1980s.<sup id="cite_ref-274" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-274">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup> Portugal subsequently has the 17th oldest population in the world, with the average age of 43.7 years.<sup id="cite_ref-275" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-275">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The structure of Portuguese society is characterized by a significant inequality which in 2016 placed the country in the lowest seventh of the <a href="/w/index.php?title=Social_Justice_Index&amp;action=edit&amp;redlink=1" class="new" title="Social Justice Index (page does not exist)">Social Justice Index</a> for the European Union.<sup id="cite_ref-276" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-276">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2018, Portugal's parliament approved a budget plan for 2019 that includes tax breaks for returning emigrants in a bid to lure back those who left during the <a href="/wiki/Financial_crisis_of_2007%E2%80%932008" class="mw-redirect" title="Financial crisis of 2007–2008">financial crisis of 2007–2008</a>. The expansionary 2019 budget, backed by a <a href="/wiki/Left-wing" class="mw-redirect" title="Left-wing">left-wing</a> majority in parliament, also aims to boost the purchasing power of households while cutting the already low deficit even further. <a href="/wiki/Circular_migration" title="Circular migration">Returning emigrants</a> will be allowed to declare only half their taxable income for five years if they return, provided they have lived abroad for at least three years. The "Return Programme" is to run for two years. Around 500,000 residents left Portugal between 2010 and 2015 after the <a href="/wiki/Great_Recession" title="Great Recession">Great Recession</a>. Although some 350,000 have since returned, this scheme aims to encourage more to return – a similar scheme exists in <a href="/wiki/Ireland" title="Ireland">Ireland</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-277" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-277">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup> Portugal has approved a credit line for Portuguese emigrants aiming to invest in the country on their return. Furthermore, emigrants returning in 2019 and 2020 will see their taxes halved as part of the stimulus to bring native Portuguese back and revitalize the population and promote continued economic growth<sup id="cite_ref-278" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-278">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup> – as Portugal struggles with a low birth rate and an <a href="/wiki/Ageing_population" class="mw-redirect" title="Ageing population">ageing population</a>. According to projections by the national statistics office, Portugal's population will fall to 7.7 million by 2080 from 10.3 million now and the population will continue to age.<sup id="cite_ref-279" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-279">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Urbanization">Urbanization</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=38" title="Edit section: Urbanization">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<p>Based on commuting patterns, OECD and Eurostat define eight <a href="/wiki/Metropolitan_areas_of_Portugal" class="mw-redirect" title="Metropolitan areas of Portugal">metropolitan areas of Portugal</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-280" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-280">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup> Only two have populations over 1 million, and since the 2013 local government reform, these are the only two which also have administrative legal status of metropolitan areas: <a href="/wiki/Lisbon_metropolitan_area" title="Lisbon metropolitan area">Lisbon</a> and <a href="/wiki/Greater_Metropolitan_Area_of_Porto" class="mw-redirect" title="Greater Metropolitan Area of Porto">Porto</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-law75_281-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-law75-281">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-oliveira_282-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-oliveira-282">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup> Several smaller metropolitan areas (<a href="/wiki/Greater_Metropolitan_Area_of_the_Algarve" class="mw-redirect" title="Greater Metropolitan Area of the Algarve">Algarve</a>, <a href="/wiki/Greater_Metropolitan_Area_of_Aveiro" class="mw-redirect" title="Greater Metropolitan Area of Aveiro">Aveiro</a>, <a href="/wiki/Greater_Metropolitan_Area_of_Coimbra" class="mw-redirect" title="Greater Metropolitan Area of Coimbra">Coimbra</a>, <a href="/wiki/Greater_Metropolitan_Area_of_Minho" title="Greater Metropolitan Area of Minho">Minho</a> and <a href="/wiki/Greater_Metropolitan_Area_of_Viseu" class="mw-redirect" title="Greater Metropolitan Area of Viseu">Viseu</a>),<sup id="cite_ref-oliveira_282-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-oliveira-282">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup> also held this status from 2003 to 2008, when they were converted into <a href="/wiki/Intermunicipal_communities_of_Portugal" title="Intermunicipal communities of Portugal">intermunicipal communities</a>, whose territories are (roughly) based on the <a href="/wiki/Nomenclature_of_Territorial_Units_for_Statistics" title="Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics">NUTS III</a> statistical regions.<sup id="cite_ref-law45_283-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-law45-283">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-oliveira_282-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-oliveira-282">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1148739982">.mw-parser-output .largestCities-table-background{background:#f9f9f9}.mw-parser-output .largestCities-cell-background{background:#f0f0f0}</style>
</p>

<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Immigration">Immigration</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=39" title="Edit section: Immigration">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Immigration_to_Portugal" title="Immigration to Portugal">Immigration to Portugal</a></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Foreigners_in_Portugal.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Foreigners_in_Portugal.png/254px-Foreigners_in_Portugal.png" decoding="async" width="254" height="132" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Foreigners_in_Portugal.png/381px-Foreigners_in_Portugal.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Foreigners_in_Portugal.png/508px-Foreigners_in_Portugal.png 2x" data-file-width="2192" data-file-height="1135" /></a><figcaption>Foreigners living in Portugal as of 2022 by country of origin. Only communities with 1,000+ residents are shown.<sup id="cite_ref-285" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-285">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>As of 2022, Portugal has 10,467,366 inhabitants, of whom about 781,915 are legal resident foreigners.<sup id="cite_ref-286" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-286">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-287" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-287">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup> Resident foreigners now make up approximately 7.47% of the population. These figures do not include people of foreign descent, as it is illegal to collect data based on ethnicity in Portugal. For instance, more than 300,000 people who have acquired <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_nationality_law" title="Portuguese nationality law">Portuguese citizenship</a> between 2008 and 2021 aren't taken into account in immigration figures as they are Portuguese citizens.<sup id="cite_ref-288" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-288">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> In 2021 alone, almost 25,000 residents of foreign origin acquired <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_passport" title="Portuguese passport">Portuguese citizenship</a>, of which 12,666 were female and 11,850 were male.<sup id="cite_ref-289" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-289">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Portugal's <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_Empire" title="Portuguese Empire">colonial history</a> has long since been a cornerstone of its national identity, as has its geographic position at the south-western corner of Europe, looking out into the Atlantic Ocean. It was one of the last western colonial European powers to give up its overseas territories (among them <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_West_Africa" class="mw-redirect" title="Portuguese West Africa">Angola</a> and <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_East_Africa" class="mw-redirect" title="Portuguese East Africa">Mozambique</a>, <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_Colonial_War" title="Portuguese Colonial War">which gained independence in 1975</a>), turning over the administration of <a href="/wiki/Macau" title="Macau">Macau</a> to the People's Republic of China at the end of 1999. Consequently, it has both influenced and been influenced by cultures from former colonies or dependencies, resulting in immigration from these former territories for both economic and personal reasons. An estimated 800,000 Portuguese returned to Portugal as the country's African possessions gained independence in 1975.<sup id="cite_ref-diaspora_290-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-diaspora-290">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Portugal, long a country of emigration (the vast majority of <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_Brazilian" class="mw-redirect" title="Portuguese Brazilian">Brazilians</a> have Portuguese ancestry),<sup id="cite_ref-diaspora_290-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-diaspora-290">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup> has now become a country of net immigration,<sup id="cite_ref-291" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-291">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup> and not just from the last <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_India" title="Portuguese India">Indian</a> (Portuguese until 1961), <a href="/wiki/Portuguese-speaking_African_countries" title="Portuguese-speaking African countries">African</a> (Portuguese until 1975), and <a href="/wiki/Macau" title="Macau">Far East Asian</a> (Portuguese until 1999) overseas territories.
</p><p>Since the 1990s, along with a boom in <a href="/wiki/Construction" title="Construction">construction</a>, several new waves of <a href="/wiki/Ukrainians" title="Ukrainians">Ukrainian</a>, <a href="/wiki/Brazilians" title="Brazilians">Brazilian</a>, <a href="/wiki/Portuguese-speaking_African_countries" title="Portuguese-speaking African countries">Lusophone Africans</a> and other <a href="/wiki/African_diaspora" title="African diaspora">Africans</a> have settled in the country. <a href="/wiki/Romanian_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Romanian people">Romanians</a>, <a href="/wiki/Moldovans" title="Moldovans">Moldovans</a>, <a href="/wiki/Kosovo_Albanians" title="Kosovo Albanians">Kosovo Albanians</a>, <a href="/wiki/Russian_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Russian people">Russians</a> and <a href="/wiki/Chinese_people" title="Chinese people">Chinese</a> have also migrated to the country. Portugal's <a href="/wiki/Romani_people" title="Romani people">Romani</a> population is estimated to be at about 52,000.<sup id="cite_ref-292" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-292">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Numbers of <a href="/wiki/Venezuelan_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Venezuelan people">Venezuelan</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pakistani_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Pakistani people">Pakistani</a> and <a href="/wiki/Indian_people" title="Indian people">Indian</a> migrants are also significant. It is estimated that over 30,000 seasonal, often <a href="/wiki/Illegal_immigrants" class="mw-redirect" title="Illegal immigrants">illegal immigrants</a> work in <a href="/wiki/Agriculture" title="Agriculture">agriculture</a>, mainly southern cities such as <a href="/wiki/Odemira" title="Odemira">Odemira</a> where they are often exploited by organized seasonal workers' networks. The workers sometimes get paid less than half the legal minimum wage. These migrants, who often arrive without due documentation or work contracts, make up over 90% of agricultural workers in the south of Portugal. Most are Indo-Asians, from India, <a href="/wiki/Bangladesh" title="Bangladesh">Bangladesh</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nepal" title="Nepal">Nepal</a>, Pakistan and <a href="/wiki/Thailand" title="Thailand">Thailand</a>. In the interior of the <a href="/wiki/Alentejo" title="Alentejo">Alentejo</a> there are many African workers. Significant numbers also come from Eastern Europe, Moldova, Ukraine, Romania and Brazil.<sup id="cite_ref-293" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-293">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In addition, a number of <a href="/wiki/EU_citizen" class="mw-redirect" title="EU citizen">EU citizens</a>, mostly from <a href="/wiki/Italy" title="Italy">Italy</a>, <a href="/wiki/France" title="France">France</a>, <a href="/wiki/Germany" title="Germany">Germany</a> or other northern European countries, have become permanent residents in the country.<sup id="cite_ref-294" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-294">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup> There is also a large expatriate community made up of <a href="/wiki/British_people" title="British people">Britons</a>, <a href="/wiki/Canadians" title="Canadians">Canadians</a> and <a href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">people from the United States of America</a>. The British community is mostly composed of retired <a href="/wiki/Pensioner" title="Pensioner">pensioners</a> who live in the Algarve and Madeira.<sup id="cite_ref-295" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-295">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Religion">Religion</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=40" title="Edit section: Religion">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>

color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Eastern_Orthodoxy" title="Eastern Orthodoxy">Eastern Orthodoxy</a> (0.69%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Pink; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;Other Christian (1.04%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Green; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Islam" title="Islam">Islam</a> (0.42%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Orange; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Hinduism" title="Hinduism">Hinduism</a> (0.22%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Gold; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Buddhism" title="Buddhism">Buddhism</a> (0.19%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Blue; color:white;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Judaism" title="Judaism">Judaism</a> (0.03%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Gray; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;Other religion (0.28%)</div><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r981673959"><div class="legend"><span class="legend-color mw-no-invert" style="background-color:Honeydew; color:black;">&#160;</span>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Irreligious" class="mw-redirect" title="Irreligious">No religion</a> (14.09%)</div>
</div>
</div></div>
<p>Roman Catholicism, which has a long history in Portugal, remains the dominant religion. Portugal has no official religion, though in the past, the <a href="/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_Portugal" title="Catholic Church in Portugal">Catholic Church in Portugal</a> was the <a href="/wiki/State_religion" title="State religion">state religion</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-296" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-296">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-297" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-297">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to the 2021 Census, 80.2% of the Portuguese population was <a href="/wiki/Catholic_Church" title="Catholic Church">Roman Catholic Christian</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Censos2021_5-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Censos2021-5">&#91;4&#93;</a></sup> The country has small Protestant, <a href="/wiki/The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints" title="The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints">Latter-day Saint</a>, <a href="/wiki/Islam_in_Portugal" title="Islam in Portugal">Muslim</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hinduism_in_Portugal" title="Hinduism in Portugal">Hindu</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sikh" class="mw-redirect" title="Sikh">Sikh</a>, <a href="/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church" title="Eastern Orthodox Church">Eastern Orthodox Church</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jehovah%27s_Witnesses" title="Jehovah&#39;s Witnesses">Jehovah's Witnesses</a>, <a href="/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_Faith" title="Baháʼí Faith">Baháʼí</a>, <a href="/wiki/Buddhism" title="Buddhism">Buddhist</a>, <a href="/wiki/Judaism" title="Judaism">Jewish</a> and <a href="/wiki/Spiritism" title="Spiritism">Spiritist</a> communities. Influences from <a href="/wiki/African_Traditional_Religion" class="mw-redirect" title="African Traditional Religion">African Traditional Religion</a> and Chinese Traditional Religion are also felt among many people, particularly in fields related with Traditional Chinese Medicine and Traditional African Herbal Medicine. Some 14.1% of the population declared themselves to be non-religious.<sup id="cite_ref-Censos2021_5-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Censos2021-5">&#91;4&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Many Portuguese holidays, festivals and traditions have a Christian origin or connotation. Although relations between the Portuguese state and the Roman Catholic Church were generally amiable and stable since the earliest years of the Portuguese nation, their relative power fluctuated. In the <a href="/wiki/History_of_Portugal_(1279-1415)" class="mw-redirect" title="History of Portugal (1279-1415)">13th and 14th centuries</a>, the church enjoyed power and close identification with early Portuguese nationalism and the foundation of the Portuguese educational system, including its <a href="/wiki/University_of_Coimbra" title="University of Coimbra">first university</a>.
</p><p>The growth of the <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_Empire" title="Portuguese Empire">Portuguese overseas empire</a> made its <a href="/wiki/Mission_(Christian)" class="mw-redirect" title="Mission (Christian)">missionaries</a> important agents of <a href="/wiki/Colonization" title="Colonization">colonization</a>, with important roles in the <a href="/wiki/Teaching" title="Teaching">education</a> and <a href="/wiki/Evangelization" class="mw-redirect" title="Evangelization">evangelization</a> of people from all the inhabited continents. The growth of <a href="/wiki/Liberal_Revolution_of_1820" title="Liberal Revolution of 1820">liberal</a> and nascent <a href="/wiki/Republicanism" title="Republicanism">republican</a> movements during the eras leading to the formation of the <a href="/wiki/First_Portuguese_Republic" title="First Portuguese Republic">First Portuguese Republic</a> (1910–26) changed the role and importance of organized religion.
</p><p>Portugal is a <a href="/wiki/Secular_state" title="Secular state">secular state</a>: <a href="/wiki/Separation_of_church_and_state" title="Separation of church and state">church and state were formally separated</a> during the First Portuguese Republic, and this was reiterated in the 1976 <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_Constitution" class="mw-redirect" title="Portuguese Constitution">Portuguese Constitution</a>. Other than the Constitution, the two most important documents relating to <a href="/wiki/Religious_freedom" class="mw-redirect" title="Religious freedom">religious freedom</a> in Portugal are the 1940 Concordata (later amended in 1971) between Portugal and the <a href="/wiki/Holy_See" title="Holy See">Holy See</a> and the 2001 Religious Freedom Act.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Languages">Languages</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=41" title="Edit section: Languages">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Languages_of_Portugal" title="Languages of Portugal">Languages of Portugal</a> and <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_language" title="Portuguese language">Portuguese language</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Gen%C3%ADsio04.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Gen%C3%ADsio04.jpg/220px-Gen%C3%ADsio04.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="121" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Gen%C3%ADsio04.jpg/330px-Gen%C3%ADsio04.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Gen%C3%ADsio04.jpg/440px-Gen%C3%ADsio04.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="880" /></a><figcaption>A sign in <a href="/wiki/Mirandese_language" title="Mirandese language">Mirandese</a> in <a href="/wiki/Miranda_do_Douro" title="Miranda do Douro">Miranda do Douro</a>, <a href="/wiki/Tr%C3%A1s-os-Montes_e_Alto_Douro_Province" title="Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro Province">Trás-os-Montes</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Portuguese is the official language of Portugal. It is a <a href="/wiki/Romance_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Romance language">Romance language</a> that is derived from <a href="/wiki/Galician-Portuguese" title="Galician-Portuguese">Galician-Portuguese</a>, which was spoken in what is now <a href="/wiki/Galicia_(Spain)" title="Galicia (Spain)">Galicia</a> and <a href="/wiki/Northern_Portugal" class="mw-redirect" title="Northern Portugal">Northern Portugal</a>. There are still strong similarities between the <a href="/wiki/Galicians" title="Galicians">Galician</a> and <a href="/wiki/Portuguese_people" title="Portuguese people">Portuguese</a> cultures. Galicia is a consultative observer of the <a href="/wiki/Community_of_Portuguese_Language_Countries" title="Community of Portuguese Language Countries">Community of Portuguese Language Countries</a>.
</p><p>The Portuguese language is derived from the <a href="/wiki/Latin_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Latin language">Latin</a> spoken by the <a href="/wiki/Romanization_(cultural)" title="Romanization (cultural)">romanized</a> <a href="/wiki/Pre-Roman_peoples_of_the_Iberian_Peninsula" class="mw-redirect" title="Pre-Roman peoples of the Iberian Peninsula">pre-Roman peoples of the Iberian Peninsula</a> around 2000 years ago – particularly the <a href="/wiki/Celts" title="Celts">Celts</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_28-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-28">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Conii" class="mw-redirect" title="Conii">Conii</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-298" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-298">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Lusitanians" title="Lusitanians">Lusitanians</a><sup id="cite_ref-academia.edu_27-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-academia.edu-27">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Turduli" title="Turduli">Turduli</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-299" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-299">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup>
In the 15th and 16th centuries, the language spread worldwide as Portugal established a colonial and commercial empire between 1415 and 1999.<sup id="cite_ref-300" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-300">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup>
Portuguese is spoken as a native language in five different continents, with Brazil accounting for the largest number of native Portuguese speakers of any country.
In 2013 the Portuguese language is the official language spoken in Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, Guinea-Bissau, Equatorial Guinea, and <a href="/wiki/East_Timor" title="East Timor">East Timor</a>. These countries, plus <a href="/wiki/Macau" title="Macau">Macau</a> Special Administrative Region (People's Republic of China) where Portuguese is co-official with <a href="/wiki/Cantonese" title="Cantonese">Cantonese</a>, make up the <a href="/wiki/Lusosphere" class="mw-redirect" title="Lusosphere">Lusosphere</a>, a term derived from the ancient <a href="/wiki/Roman_province" title="Roman province">Roman province</a> of "<a href="/wiki/Lusitania" title="Lusitania">Lusitania</a>", which currently matches the Portuguese territory south of the <a href="/wiki/Douro" title="Douro">Douro</a> river.<sup id="cite_ref-301" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-301">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Mirandese_language" title="Mirandese language">Mirandese</a> is also recognized as a co-official regional language in some municipalities of North-Eastern Portugal. It is part of the <a href="/wiki/Astur-Leonese" class="mw-redirect" title="Astur-Leonese">Astur-Leonese</a> group of languages.<sup id="cite_ref-302" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-302">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup> An estimate of between 6,000 and 7,000 Mirandese speakers has been documented for Portugal.<sup id="cite_ref-303" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-303">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup> Furthermore, a particular dialect known as <a href="/wiki/Barranquenho" title="Barranquenho">Barranquenho</a>, spoken in <a href="/wiki/Barrancos" title="Barrancos">Barrancos</a>, is also officially recognized and protected in Portugal since 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-304" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-304">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Minderico_language" title="Minderico language">Minderico</a>, a <a href="/wiki/Sociolect" title="Sociolect">sociolect</a> of the Portuguese language, is spoken by around 500 people in the town of <a href="/wiki/Minde,_Portugal" title="Minde, Portugal">Minde</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-305" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-305">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>According to the <a href="/wiki/EF_English_Proficiency_Index" title="EF English Proficiency Index">International English Proficiency Index</a>, Portugal has a high proficiency level in English, higher than those of other Romance-speaking European countries like Spain, Italy or France.<sup id="cite_ref-306" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-306">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Education">Education</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=42" title="Edit section: Education">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Education_in_Portugal" title="Education in Portugal">Education in Portugal</a></div>
<p>The educational system is divided into preschool (for those under age six), basic education (nine years, in three stages, compulsory), secondary education (three years, compulsory since 2010), and higher education (subdivided in university and <a href="/wiki/Polytechnic_(Portugal)" title="Polytechnic (Portugal)">polytechnic</a> education). Universities are usually organized into <a href="/wiki/Faculty_(division)" title="Faculty (division)">faculties</a>. Institutes and schools are also common designations for autonomous subdivisions of <a href="/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_Portugal" class="mw-redirect" title="List of colleges and universities in Portugal">Portuguese higher education institutions</a>.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:University_of_Evora_(36815429156).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/University_of_Evora_%2836815429156%29.jpg/220px-University_of_Evora_%2836815429156%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="147" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/University_of_Evora_%2836815429156%29.jpg/330px-University_of_Evora_%2836815429156%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/University_of_Evora_%2836815429156%29.jpg/440px-University_of_Evora_%2836815429156%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="6000" data-file-height="4000" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/University_of_%C3%89vora" title="University of Évora">University of Evora</a>, Portugal's second-oldest university</figcaption></figure>
<p>The total adult literacy rate in Portugal was 99.8% in 2021<sup id="cite_ref-307" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-307">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup> and 100% of primary school enrolments. According to the <a href="/wiki/Programme_for_International_Student_Assessment" title="Programme for International Student Assessment">Programme for International Student Assessment</a> (PISA) 2018, Portugal scored around the <a href="/wiki/OECD" title="OECD">OECD</a> average in reading, mathematics and science. In reading and mathematics, mean performance in 2018 was close to the level observed in 2009 to 2015; in science, mean performance in 2018 was below that of 2015, and returned close to the level observed in 2009 and 2012.<sup id="cite_ref-308" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-308">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-309" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-309">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>About 46,9% of college-age citizens (20 years old) attend one of Portugal's higher education institutions<sup id="cite_ref-310" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-310">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-311" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-311">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-312" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-312">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> (compared with 50% in the United States and 35% in the OECD countries). In addition to being a destination for <a href="/wiki/International_student" title="International student">international students</a>, Portugal is also among the top places of origin for international students. All higher education students, both domestic and international, totalled 380,937 in 2005.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:King_Diniz_Statue_-_Coimbra_University.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/King_Diniz_Statue_-_Coimbra_University.jpg/220px-King_Diniz_Statue_-_Coimbra_University.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/King_Diniz_Statue_-_Coimbra_University.jpg/330px-King_Diniz_Statue_-_Coimbra_University.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/King_Diniz_Statue_-_Coimbra_University.jpg/440px-King_Diniz_Statue_-_Coimbra_University.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1944" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Denis_of_Portugal" title="Denis of Portugal">King Diniz</a> statue at the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Coimbra" title="University of Coimbra">University of Coimbra</a>: the first university in Portugal (now the University of Coimbra), then called the <i><a href="/wiki/Studium_generale" title="Studium generale">Estudo Geral</a></i> (General Study), was founded in Lisbon with his signing of the document <i>Scientiae thesaurus mirabilis</i> in Leiria on 3 March 1290.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Portuguese universities have existed since 1290. The <a href="/wiki/University_of_Coimbra" title="University of Coimbra">oldest Portuguese university</a><sup id="cite_ref-313" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-313">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup> was first established in Lisbon before moving to <a href="/wiki/Coimbra" title="Coimbra">Coimbra</a>. Historically, within the scope of the Portuguese Empire, the Portuguese founded the oldest engineering school of the <a href="/wiki/Americas" title="Americas">Americas</a> (the <i><a href="/wiki/Real_Academia_de_Artilharia,_Fortifica%C3%A7%C3%A3o_e_Desenho" class="mw-redirect" title="Real Academia de Artilharia, Fortificação e Desenho">Real Academia de Artilharia, Fortificação e Desenho</a></i> of <a href="/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro" title="Rio de Janeiro">Rio de Janeiro</a>) in 1792, as well as the oldest medical college in Asia (the <i><a href="/wiki/Escola_M%C3%A9dico-Cir%C3%BArgica_de_Goa" class="mw-redirect" title="Escola Médico-Cirúrgica de Goa">Escola Médico-Cirúrgica</a></i> of <a href="/wiki/Goa" title="Goa">Goa</a>) in 1842. Presently, the largest university in Portugal is the <a href="/wiki/University_of_Lisbon" title="University of Lisbon">University of Lisbon</a>.
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Bologna_process" class="mw-redirect" title="Bologna process">Bologna process</a> has been adopted by Portuguese universities and poly-technical institutes in 2006. Higher education in state-run educational establishments is provided on a competitive basis, a system of <i><a href="/wiki/Numerus_clausus" title="Numerus clausus">numerus clausus</a></i> is enforced through a national database on student admissions. However, every higher education institution offers also a number of additional vacant places through other extraordinary admission processes for sportsmen, mature applicants (over 23 years old), <a href="/wiki/International_students" class="mw-redirect" title="International students">international students</a>, foreign students from the <a href="/wiki/Lusosphere" class="mw-redirect" title="Lusosphere">Lusosphere</a>, degree owners from other institutions, students from other institutions (<a href="/wiki/Transfer_admissions_in_the_United_States" title="Transfer admissions in the United States">academic transfer</a>), former students (readmission), and course change, which are subject to specific standards and regulations set by each institution or course department.
</p><p>Most student costs are supported with public money. However, with the increasing tuition fees a student has to pay to attend a Portuguese state-run higher education institution and the attraction of new types of students (many as international students and part-time students or in evening classes) like employees, businessmen, parents, pensioners and foreigners (most prominently from <a href="/wiki/Brazil" title="Brazil">Brazil</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-314" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-314">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup> a Portuguese-speaking country), many departments make a substantial profit from every additional student enrolled in courses, with benefits for the college or university's gross tuition revenue and without<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (November 2021)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> loss of educational quality (teacher per student, computer per student, classroom size per student, etc.).
</p><p>Portugal has entered into <a href="/wiki/Higher_education_in_Portugal#International_partnership_agreements" title="Higher education in Portugal">cooperation agreements with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and other US institutions</a> to further develop and increase the effectiveness of Portuguese higher education and research.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Health">Health</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=43" title="Edit section: Health">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Health_in_Portugal" title="Health in Portugal">Health in Portugal</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:204px;max-width:204px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a class="trow" style="display:flex"><div class="thumbcaption">St António Hospital, in <a href="/wiki/Porto" title="Porto">Porto</a> (above), and St Maria Hospital, in Lisbon (bottom)</div></div></div></div>
<p>According to the <a href="/wiki/Human_Development_Report" title="Human Development Report">Human Development Report</a>, the average <a href="/wiki/Life_expectancy" title="Life expectancy">life expectancy</a> in Portugal had reached 82 years in 2017;<sup id="cite_ref-315" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-315">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup> in 2020 it was estimated at 82.11 years.<sup id="cite_ref-316" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-316">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup> As projected by the United Nations, the life expectancy of the Portuguese population will be over 90 years when we reach 2100.<sup id="cite_ref-317" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-317">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Portugal ranks 12th in the best public health systems in the world, ahead of other countries like the United Kingdom, Germany or Sweden.<sup id="cite_ref-318" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-318">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-319" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-319">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Portuguese health system is characterized by three coexisting systems: the National Health Service (<i>Serviço Nacional de Saúde</i>, SNS), special social health insurance schemes for certain professions (health subsystems) and voluntary private health insurance. The SNS provides universal coverage. In addition, about 25% of the population is covered by the health subsystems, 10% by private insurance schemes and another 7% by mutual funds.
</p><p>The Ministry of Health is responsible for developing health policy as well as managing the SNS. Five regional health administrations are in charge of implementing the national health policy objectives, developing guidelines and protocols and supervising health care delivery. Decentralization efforts have aimed at shifting financial and management responsibility to the regional level. In practice, however, the autonomy of regional health administrations over budget setting and spending has been limited to primary care.
</p><p>The SNS is predominantly funded through general taxation. Employer (including the state) and employee contributions represent the main funding sources of the health subsystems. In addition, direct payments by the patient and voluntary health insurance premiums account for a large proportion of funding.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:FCM-UNL.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/FCM-UNL.JPG/220px-FCM-UNL.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/FCM-UNL.JPG/330px-FCM-UNL.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/FCM-UNL.JPG/440px-FCM-UNL.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1200" /></a><figcaption>The Medical Department of <a href="/wiki/NOVA_University_Lisbon" title="NOVA University Lisbon">NOVA University Lisbon</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Similar to the other Eur-A countries, most Portuguese die from <a href="/wiki/Noncommunicable_diseases" class="mw-redirect" title="Noncommunicable diseases">noncommunicable diseases</a>. Mortality from <a href="/wiki/Cardiovascular_diseases" class="mw-redirect" title="Cardiovascular diseases">cardiovascular diseases</a> (CVD) is higher than in the <a href="/wiki/Eurozone" title="Eurozone">eurozone</a>, but its two main components, ischaemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disease, display inverse trends compared with the Eur-A, with <a href="/wiki/Cerebrovascular_disease" title="Cerebrovascular disease">cerebrovascular disease</a> being the single biggest killer in Portugal (17%). Portuguese people die 12% less often from cancer than in the Eur-A, but mortality is not declining as rapidly as in the Eur-A. Cancer is more frequent among children as well as among women younger than 44 years. Although lung cancer (slowly increasing among women) and breast cancer (decreasing rapidly) are scarcer, cervical cancer and prostate cancer are more frequent.
Portugal has the highest mortality rate for diabetes in the Eur-A, with a sharp increase since the 1980s.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Hospitais_da_Universidade_de_Coimbra_-_main_entrance.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Hospitais_da_Universidade_de_Coimbra_-_main_entrance.JPG/220px-Hospitais_da_Universidade_de_Coimbra_-_main_entrance.JPG" decoding="async" width="220" height="146" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Hospitais_da_Universidade_de_Coimbra_-_main_entrance.JPG/330px-Hospitais_da_Universidade_de_Coimbra_-_main_entrance.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Hospitais_da_Universidade_de_Coimbra_-_main_entrance.JPG/440px-Hospitais_da_Universidade_de_Coimbra_-_main_entrance.JPG 2x" data-file-width="4928" data-file-height="3264" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Hospitais_da_Universidade_de_Coimbra" title="Hospitais da Universidade de Coimbra">Hospitais da Universidade de Coimbra</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Portugal's <a href="/wiki/Infant_mortality_rate" class="mw-redirect" title="Infant mortality rate">infant mortality rate</a> is around 2 deaths per 1000 newborns, with 2.4 deaths per 1000 live births.
</p><p>People are usually well informed about their health status, the positive and negative effects of their behaviour on their health, and their use of health care services. Yet their perceptions of their health, can differ from what administrative and examination-based data show about levels of illness within populations. Thus, survey results based on self-reporting at household level, complement other data on health status and the use of services.
</p><p>Only one third of adults rated their health as good or very good in Portugal (Kasmel et al., 2004). This is the lowest of the Eur-A countries reporting and reflects the relatively adverse situation of the country in terms of mortality and selected morbidity.<sup id="cite_ref-320" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-320">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Hospital_de_Santa_Maria" title="Hospital de Santa Maria">Hospital de Santa Maria</a> is the largest university hospital in Portugal.<sup id="cite_ref-321" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-321">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Culture">Culture</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=44" title="Edit section: Culture">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Culture_of_Portugal" title="Culture of Portugal">Culture of Portugal</a></div>
<p>Portugal has developed a specific culture while being influenced by various civilizations that have crossed the Mediterranean and the European continent, or were introduced when it played an active role during the <a href="/wiki/Portugal_in_the_Age_of_Discovery" class="mw-redirect" title="Portugal in the Age of Discovery">Age of Discovery</a>. In the 1990s and 2000s (decade), Portugal modernized its public cultural facilities, in addition to the <a href="/wiki/Calouste_Gulbenkian_Foundation" title="Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation">Calouste Gulbenkian Foundation</a> established in 1956 in Lisbon.
</p><p>These include the <a href="/wiki/Bel%C3%A9m_Cultural_Centre" class="mw-redirect" title="Belém Cultural Centre">Belém Cultural Centre</a> in Lisbon, <a href="/wiki/Serralves_Foundation" class="mw-redirect" title="Serralves Foundation">Serralves Foundation</a> and the <a href="/wiki/Casa_da_M%C3%BAsica" title="Casa da Música">Casa da Música</a>, both in <a href="/wiki/Porto" title="Porto">Porto</a>, as well as new public cultural facilities like municipal libraries and concert halls that were built or renovated in many municipalities across the country.
Portugal is home to <a href="/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Portugal" title="List of World Heritage Sites in Portugal">17</a> UNESCO <a href="/wiki/World_Heritage_Site" title="World Heritage Site">World Heritage Sites</a>, ranking it <a href="/wiki/World_Heritage_Sites_by_country" title="World Heritage Sites by country">9th in Europe and 18th in the world.</a>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Architecture">Architecture</span><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Portugal&amp;action=edit&amp;section=45" title="Edit section: Architecture">edit</a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Architecture_of_Portugal" class="mw-redirect" title="Architecture of Portugal">Architecture of Portugal</a> and <a href="/wiki/Classification_of_Built_Heritage_in_Portugal" title="Classification of Built Heritage in Portugal">Classification of Built Heritage in Portugal</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1096954695/mw-parser-output/.tmulti"><div class="thumb tmulti tright"><div class="thumbinner multiimageinner" style="width:204px;max-width:204px"><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Jer%C3%B3nimos_April_2009-4.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Jer%C3%B3nimos_April_2009-4.jpg/300px-Jer%C3%B3nimos_April_2009-4.jpg 1.5x, /></a></span></div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Torre_Bel%C3%A9m_April_2009-4a.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Torre_Bel%C3%A9m_April_2009-4a.jpg/300px-Torre_Bel%C3%A9m_April_2009-4a.jpg 1.5x, /></a></span></div></div></div><div class="trow"><div class="tsingle" style="width:202px;max-width:202px"><div class="thumbimage"><span typeof="mw:File"><a href="/wiki/File:Casamusicaexterior.jpg"
